unit.can_do_en: join a coffee break and accept a sauna invitation.

brief.situation_en: Leena and Maria at Leena's family cottage by a lake.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.gloss_en: Shall I throw more water on the stones?

judge.reason: Same question; only register differences (heitänks/mä vs heitänkö/minä).
vaan/vain are register variants of 'just'; same meaning.
Okei and selvä both mean 'okay'; onks/onko is register only.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Joo, ihana lämpö. Nyt mä ymmärrän, miks te tykkäätte saunast.
lines.text_kirja: Kyllä, ihana lämpö. Nyt minä ymmärrän, miksi te pidätte saunasta.
lines.gloss_en: Yes, lovely heat. Now I understand why you like the sauna.

judge.reason: Joo/kyllä both 'yes'; tykkäätte saunast and pidätte saunasta both mean 'like the sauna'; same meaning.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.text_puhe: Mennäänks kohta uimaan? Järvi on tos.
lines.text_kirja: Mennäänkö pian uimaan? Järvi on tuossa.
lines.gloss_en: Shall we go swimming soon? The lake is right there.

judge.reason: Kohta/pian both 'soon'; tos/tuossa 'over there'; same meaning.
Eiks/eikö, oo/ole, tosi/todella all register variants; same question.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.gloss_en: It is, but that's the best part!

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 1st person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Heitän (I throw) with the question ending -kö: heitänkö. Speech says heitänks.
Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.
This is how you tell someone to add: lisää. It comes from lisätä.
Adds -ä for some löyly, the steam from water on the hot stones.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech says vaan. Books write vain.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Means 'is...?'. The question ending -ko turns 'on' (is) into a question.
Means 'good!' or 'great!', showing you are happy.
Yes. In everyday speech people often say joo instead.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Means 'now'. Leo asks where home is at this time.
Ymmärtää changes to ymmärrä- and takes -n for 'I': ymmärrän.
Speech drops the last i: miks. Books write miksi.
Te is 'you' when you talk to more than one person. People say it the same way.

forms.lemma_meaning_en: to have to, to like, to hold
forms.why_en: From pitää, to like. Books write te pidätte. Speech uses tykätä and says tykkäätte.
Pitää and tykätä (to like) want -sta: sauna becomes saunasta. Speech drops the a: saunast.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, passive, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Mennään, let's go, with -kö to ask. Speech says -ks: mennäänks.
Speech often says kohta 'in a moment' instead of pian.
Uida takes -maan after mennä (to go): mennä uimaan means 'to go swimming'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Means 'is': present tense, 3rd person singular, going with 'Helsinki'.
Tuo, that, with -ssa: tuossa, there. Speech says tos.

forms.form_name_en: negative verb, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Ei (not) with the question ending: eikö. Speech says eiks. Eikö niin? asks 'isn't that so?'
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The partitive singular matches vettä: kylmä becomes kylmää.
Means 'but'. It links two ideas: from Tampere, but home is in Helsinki.
'It.' Nominative singular, referring back to the price.
Uskaltaa changes to uskalla- and takes -n for 'I': uskallan.
